keyVerseText: In the end of the sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week, came Mary Magdalene and the other Mary to see the sepulchre.
rootMeaning: The Greek adverb ὀψέ (opsé) derives from the same root as ὀπίσω (opísō), which carries the idea of moving backward or after something in time or place. This etymological connection highlights a fundamental sense of lateness or coming after a certain point, emphasizing a temporal delay or occurrence subsequent to an event. Unlike the simple English glosses 'even' or 'late,' the root sense conveys a notion of backwardness or following, which enriches our understanding of its temporal nuance.
usageInScripture: With only three occurrences in the New Testament, ὀψέ consistently conveys the idea of lateness or the time toward the end of a day or period. Its primary translations as 'even' or 'at even' reflect a consistent usage related to the close of the day or the end of a significant time frame. This focused semantic range underscores its role in marking a moment that is not immediate but comes after a considerable passage of time, often carrying a sense of culmination or transition.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ὀψέ as denoting 'late' or 'after' enriches our grasp of biblical events that unfold in divinely appointed timing rather than human immediacy. This word reminds believers that God's purposes often come to fruition 'in the end' or 'at the close' of a period, emphasizing patience and trust in His sovereign schedule. It also points to the fulfillment of prophecy and promise not at the beginning but at the appointed time, reinforcing the faithfulness of God to act precisely when He wills. Recognizing this temporal dimension encourages believers to wait with hope and perseverance, confident that God's timing is perfect.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 28:1, the phrase 'In the end of the sabbath' uses ὀψέ to mark the moment when Mary Magdalene and the other Mary come to the tomb, signaling a transition from the sacred rest of the sabbath to the dawn of the first day of the week. The word highlights that this event occurs not just after the sabbath but at its conclusion, emphasizing the significance of timing in the resurrection narrative. It invites reflection on how God's redemptive work unfolds at the appointed moment, bringing new beginnings out of endings.
